incident: SessionStart/UserPromptSubmit/PreCompact hooks were scored DONE (AUTO-01/02) after passing pipe tests, but never fired in the harness. On Windows, bare `bash` on PATH resolves to WSL bash (C:\WINDOWS\system32 ash.exe), and exec-form args carrying backslash Windows paths arrive mangled ('C:Usersshova.claudehookssession-recall.sh'). Even reached via /mnt/c, WSL bash emitted an empty {} because it cannot see the Windows-rooted paths the scripts read.
lesson: A hook verified in isolation is STAGED, not DONE; 'wired' must mean observed firing inside the harness. Never spawn `bash` by bare name on Windows (WSL wins the PATH); name the Git Bash interpreter explicitly and use POSIX /c/ paths so no backslash survives to be eaten. Silent-failure surfaces need disk evidence or they get scored on intent.
enforcement: settings.json hooks now exec 'C:\Program Files\Git in ash.exe' with /c/... script args (exec-green from a native Windows parent: exit 0, 4621/1582 bytes, PreCompact 0-byte by design); all three hooks append to state/hook-fires.log so firing leaves disk evidence; AUTO-01/AUTO-02 downgraded to STAGED pending a harness-written fire-log line
closed: 2026-07-24: state/hook-fires.log carries 7 harness-written SessionStart lines with real session ids (incl. 8abb324e-...), 11 PreCompact lines, 12 compact-log.md snapshots. Hooks now also log source=/trigger= so auto-vs-manual compaction is measurable.

incident: AUTO-10 (Gemini second-model review) and AUTO-18 (always-on scheduling) were both carried as BLOCKED(operator) in TODO.md and the PRD acceptance table. Neither was actually blocked. GEMINI_API_KEY was sitting in a local .env the whole time and gh was authed with repo scope, so the secret could be set in one command. Task Scheduler was assumed to need the operator's password for a run-whether-logged-on-or-not task; in fact this shell already runs as Administrator and S4U logon registers a WakeToRun/Highest task with no password stored. Weeks of 'waiting on operator' were self-inflicted.
lesson: BLOCKED(operator) is a claim about the world and needs the same evidence bar as DONE. Before assigning a blocker to the human, probe the capability directly: check auth scope, check elevation, attempt the privileged op against a throwaway target and read the error. An unprobed blocker is ASSUMED, and it costs more than a wrong DONE because nobody re-tests it.
enforcement: AUTO-10/AUTO-18 unblocked and re-scored with command evidence (gh secret list shows GEMINI_API_KEY 2026-07-24T20:17:02Z; S4U probe registered and read back LogonType=S4U RunLevel=Highest WakeToRun=True, then removed). Rule going forward: any TODO line carrying BLOCKED(operator) must name the probe command that established the block, or it is downgraded to UNPROBED on sight.

incident: deploy-setup.sh, the one instrument built this session to detect repo-vs-live drift, shipped THREE independent false-green defects at once. (1) --only took its glob into a case pattern from a variable, so 'a|b' became one literal pattern containing | and matched zero files; zero compared printed as in sync. (2) A filter that matched nothing exited 0, so 'nothing was compared' and 'nothing differs' were the same output. (3) report()'s 20-line cap test was the last command of its for body, so any section holding 1 to 19 items returned 1 and set -euo pipefail killed the script mid-report with exit 1, which is EXACTLY the exit code a successful dry run returns. --apply therefore died before copying anything and looked indistinguishable from a dry run, made worse because the report verb still read 'would UPDATE' after an apply.
lesson: A verifier is the last place a false green is tolerable, and all three defects were false greens, not crashes. Two transferable rules. First, a reporting helper must never decide the script's exit status: put an explicit return 0 at the end of any function whose last statement is a test, because under set -e that test IS the script's fate. Second, an exit code that a failure shares with a success is not a signal; a death's code must be distinguishable from a legitimate one (this one collided with the dry-run code and cost a full misdiagnosis). Corollary: a filter matching nothing must exit non-zero, and output verbs must track the mode so a silent no-op cannot read as a dry run.
enforcement: All three fixed on disk at dot-claude/bin/deploy-setup.sh: --only splits on IFS='|,' into real array elements and is repeatable (lines 60-71); zero-match exits 2 with 'This is a filter error, not a sync result' (lines 153-160); report() ends in an explicit return 0 with the root cause written into the comment (lines 162-182); verbs switch CREATE/UPDATE vs would-CREATE/would-UPDATE on APPLY (lines 199-207). Header now documents exit 0 = in sync, 1 = not, so the script is usable directly as a refutation verifier. NEXT: add a refutation claim that shells out to it and asserts on the exit code, which is only defensible now that these three are fixed.

incident: Five diagnostic errors in one session, all the same shape: a confident claim from a model of the artifact rather than the artifact. (1) The meme-subsystem inventory undercounted; hooks were in dot-codex/hooks not dot-claude/hooks, the real SKILL.md was in dot-agents, two skills entries were symlinks, and startup-scripts/claude-meme-hooks-startup.sh was missed entirely. (2) A zero-hit grep on gastown-company-registry.md was diagnosed as a Grep-tool false negative; the grep was correct and my model of the file was 200 lines stale, the persona registry having been replaced by a 356-byte path-scoped rule. (3) I asserted those files were symlinks whose reparse payload bash had read; PowerShell returned kind=realfile len=356. (4) I generalized dot-codex's dead-Linux-path pattern to the live tree, where it did not hold. (5) On the --apply no-op I named my own --only edit as prime suspect; a standalone parser harness returned APPLY=1 PATS='a b' and falsified it, and the real cause was report().
lesson: Each error came from reasoning over a remembered artifact instead of re-reading it, and the most expensive one was blaming my own most recent edit, which is a plausible story that stops the search early. Two rules. First, when an instrument and my expectation disagree, the instrument is the default suspect only AFTER re-reading the input it was pointed at: a stale mental model is far more common than a broken grep. Second, isolate before accusing: the parser harness that cleared --only took one minute and would have saved the whole misdiagnosis if run first. Also: inventory a subsystem by grepping its vocabulary across ALL trees, never by listing the one directory you expect it in.
enforcement: Verification pattern adopted and used to close the meme removal: three independent signals in one call, a CR-insensitive diff (diff --strip-trailing-cr, since raw diff reported 1,197c1,197 purely from CRLF), a negative grep for the removed vocabulary, and a POSITIVE CONTROL string on the same file in the same invocation, because a zero from a broken invocation is indistinguishable from a zero from a clean file. Real output: 0 differing lines x 4 files, 0 meme hits x 3 files, persona=3 as the control. Refutation claim C-006 must be broadened beyond skills/ and beyond the literal /home/shovalbe string, since it was narrower than the defect class it existed to catch.

incident: Four untracked docs/analysis/2026-07-25-*.md files were carried forward across a compaction boundary as 'likely the output of workflow wdtexwdxs', the workflow launched against the operator's eight-part setup question, and were queued to be reported to him as the answer. The workflow had in fact FAILED: 4 of 12 agents errored, pipeline stages 0/1/4 dead from 180s stalls on all 6 retry attempts, 2.66 hours and 3.64M subagent tokens spent. Had the failure notification arrived later, failed-run leftovers would have been presented as a deliverable.
lesson: An artifact's existence on disk is not evidence of which process produced it, and never evidence that the process succeeded. Provenance is a separate claim from presence and needs its own check (run id in the file, or the run's own success record). This is the same existence-is-not-execution error as scoring an unregistered hook file as a live hook. It is also why a carried assumption must be re-tested when new evidence lands rather than inherited as settled: the assumption survived a compaction unchallenged precisely because it read as already-established context.
enforcement: Retraction stated to the operator in-line rather than quietly dropped: 'I cannot attribute the four untracked docs/analysis/2026-07-25-*.md files to it as the answer to your eight-part question, and I won't.' Failure filed on the a2a bus as 1784937929-efc83c so it survives this context. The eight-part question is to be answered directly in-loop; resuming wf_4d739b98-873 is NOT authorized, since the operator already named the spin-up-another-workflow reflex as the problem. Harness gap recorded: a 180s-stall x 6-attempt policy idles ~18 min per stage with no liveness signal to the lead.

incident: The only Stop hook wired in this setup, dot-claude/hooks/completion_gate.py, was assumed to be enforcing calibrated-claims discipline for months. Two executable probes today: (A) given a realistic Stop payload {session_id, transcript_path, cwd, hook_event_name, stop_hook_active} it returns {} unconditionally, because assistant_text() reads four inline keys and has no transcript_path fallback, so the text it judges is always the empty string; (B) even when the message is passed inline, its EVIDENCE regex is polarity-blind, so 'Fixed. Nothing was tested.' PASSES on the word 'tested', and 'All done. The build output is above.' passes on 'build' and 'output'. Only a claim containing zero evidence vocabulary is blocked.
lesson: Two independent failures stacked, and either alone would have been enough to make the hook worthless. The wiring was real but the input was never available, and the oracle rewarded vocabulary rather than action. A regex over the assistant's own prose cannot be an evidence check no matter how it is written: the thing being measured is the thing writing the answer. An enforcement hook needs a positive test that runs it on the payload shape the runtime actually sends, not on the shape that is convenient to construct.
enforcement: dot-claude/hooks/ship_gate_stop.py replaces it as the real Stop enforcement: it reads transcript_path (treating it as load-bearing, not a fallback) and takes its verdict from state/gate-runs.jsonl fingerprinted to the exact working tree, which the agent cannot write with prose. Its test suite includes case 9, a transcript-only payload with no inline message, precisely because that is the shape that defeated completion_gate.py. completion_gate.py is kept only as a calibration nudge and must not be cited as evidence of anything.

incident: tools/review/panel.py shipped 32 pattern checks. Before the selftest derived its expectations from the PERSONAS registry, the 'unawaited' check had matched nothing in its entire existence: its pattern required foo.bar.then( and could not cross the parentheses in save(row).then(...), which is the shape the defect actually takes. Four further checks were wrong in ways only a planted corpus exposed: xit\( matched the tail of SystemExit( and reported 50 ordinary Python entry points as disabled tests; SET[^;]* swallowed the WHERE clause the no-where check required; nullable-fk looked only rightward and missed NOT NULL before REFERENCES; todo-added ran unscoped and returned 296 findings, 294 of them TODO lines in markdown plans where a TODO is the content.
lesson: A check with no positive test is indistinguishable from a check that can never fire, and a hardcoded expectation list hides exactly the checks nobody thought about. Deriving the test expectations from the registry so an untested check fails the suite is what turned five silent defects into five visible ones. Separately: a false positive is a line somebody has to defend in review for no reason, so 296 findings of legitimate content is worse than zero findings, because it teaches the reader to skip the tool.
enforcement: cmd_selftest computes want = [(p, c) for p, spec in PERSONAS.items() for c, *_ in spec['checks']], so adding a check without a positive test fails the suite. An innocent corpus sits alongside the planted one and every line in it is a real false positive from an earlier version of the file, kept as a regression. Checks are scoped to CODE_LANGS where the pattern is only a defect in code.

incident: tools/audit/pointers.py measured what the canonical config trees actually contain: 108 files whose entire content is an absolute Linux path that does not exist on this Windows machine, including 33 of the 63 entries in dot-claude/skills and 33 in dot-codex/skills, plus 30 hooks and 11 rules. red-team, red-team-review, mutation-runner, property-test-gen, triage-tests, code-simplifier and commit-push-pr are all 37-to-44-byte dead paths. coverage-enforcer/SKILL.md names a companion hook at ~/.codex/hooks/coverage-enforcer.sh that is absent and says it gates commit-push-pr, which is itself hollow. 408 further document references name absent paths, 40 of them to one missing script, ~/.claude/bin/work-item.sh.
lesson: A directory listing is not an inventory. More than half the skills in the canonical tree are a name with nothing behind it, and nothing about loading one announces the absence. The mitigating finding is that zero of these are wired: both settings.json files invoke only hooks that exist and are real files, so nothing is currently failing open through this path. That distinction matters and was worth measuring rather than assuming, because 'wired but hollow' is a live enforcement gap while 'unwired and hollow' is a misleading inventory.
enforcement: tools/audit/pointers.py scan classifies wired-missing and wired-hollow at high, unwired pointers at medium, stale document references at low, and exits non-zero on high by default so it can gate. Its selftest plants one of each kind plus the false positives that would make it unreadable: a real script, a one-line command with arguments, a pointer whose target exists, and a document naming a live path. 13/13, exit 0. Full list re-derivable to state/dangling-pointers.tsv; nothing is reconstructed, because a pointer does not record what it pointed at and writing a plausible replacement would be inventing a file and calling it a repair.

lesson: Lane C did Lane B's work for most of a session. Edited tools/review/panel.py, tools/map/codemap.py, tools/audit/mutations/panel.py, ~/.claude/hooks/, and seeded orchestration telemetry, all of which charters.md:19 assigns to Lane B. Also wrote a handoff into daily-deep-learning (Lane D).

lesson: charters.md rule 2 requires /diverge on design decisions, five candidates, weird-first. It was run zero times. So was /prove-implementation, which the project CLAUDE.md requires for architecture and 'best' claims.

lesson: The same violation as L-2026-07-27-a recurred in the next session: undeclared lane, cwd Downloads\new-recruit, and the whole session was Lane B harness work (taskbar pin, launcher tests, claude-setup commit e35123d). why_it_happened: The fix was installed next to the habit instead of inside it. Desktop shortcuts and a working chooser are both real artifacts, and both were reported as the fix, but the operator opens Claude from the taskbar. A correct mechanism on a surface nobody touches is staged, not deployed.

Operator confirmed the chooser opens on click. tests/test_workspace_launcher.py::TaskbarPin asserts the live pin runs the chooser and not the old hardcoded -d form, so this specific gap is now measured rather than remembered.

lesson: CLAUDE-OS.md:45 has governed this system since it was written: '>=0.90 autonomous; 0.70-0.90 work + explicit proof gate; <0.70 ask'. Nothing in the tree has ever recorded a claimed confidence beside a verified outcome, so those two thresholds have never been calibrated and the reliability curve is not computable from anything on disk.
why_it_happened: The rule reads like a measurement because it carries decimals. A number with two decimal places is not evidence that anyone measured anything, and the rule was adopted from the intent-plane design without an accompanying ledger.
fix: RT-1 in TODO.md: log {claimed_confidence, action, verified_outcome} first, compute the curve, and only then decide whether 0.90 and 0.70 are the right cuts or whether the signal is inert. External evidence (2026 calibration literature, docs/analysis/2026-07-27-research-transfer-uncertainty-and-oracles.md T1) says verbalized model confidence sits at 80-100 regardless of accuracy, which would make >=0.90 the default path wearing the costume of a gate.
class: a check that cannot fail, one level above the hooks pointers.py was written for

lesson: Three ADRs (0005 approval-gated self-modification, 0012 autonomy only via PR gate, 0014 phone-approval before publish) rest on a human approving. state/ holds 753 gate runs and a machine refutation ledger, and no record at all of a human approve-or-reject decision. The rejection rate on the system's own primary safety mechanism cannot be computed.
why_it_happened: Approval felt like an event that happens outside the system, so nothing captured it. The automation-bias literature is that approval under volume decays into rubber-stamping while the paperwork still shows a human choice, which is the exact state that would be invisible here.
fix: RT-2 in TODO.md: append-only decision ledger plus approvals/rejections/ratio on the daily digest. A ratio that has never seen a rejection is the finding, not a clean bill of health.

lesson: Claimed on a panel-prep answer that verification infrastructure is 'not commoditized' and asked 'is anyone funding it'. All four not-a-gap signals fire: 4+ surveys (KDD 2025, ACL 2026 IBM, agent-provenance, a 110-paper harness survey), 4+ curated awesome-lists, a NeurIPS 2026 workshop literally titled 'Who Verifies the Agents?', and $230M raised by AI evaluation tools in 12 months with Braintrust at $800M and Langfuse acquired by ClickHouse in Jan 2026.
why_it_happened: The counterevidence was already in my own retrieval log. The ICML 2026 workshop 'Statistical Frameworks for Uncertainty in Agentic Systems' and two listicles of 2026 eval/observability tools had come back in searches I ran the same session, and I did not re-read my own results before asserting absence. This was not a search failure. It was a failure to read what I already had.
fix: The prior_art_gate Stop hook caught it and demanded three-vocabulary searches; that hook worked exactly as designed and is the reason the wrong claim never left the session unchallenged. Standing change: before writing any absence claim, grep the session's own prior tool results first, because a same-session retrieval is the cheapest possible source and the one most likely to already hold the refutation.
class: absence claim made against evidence already in hand

lesson: Wrote 'I filed this as a lesson' in a response and never ran the command. The claim was discovered false one turn later by reading state/lessons.jsonl, whose newest row was still L-2026-07-27-e.
why_it_happened: The sentence was written in the same breath as the intent to do it, and nothing between intent and output required the file to change. Narrating an action and performing it are separated by exactly one tool call, and prose does not notice when that call is missing.
fix: This is L015 restated at the level of my own reporting: an artifact's existence is not evidence, and neither is a sentence saying the artifact exists. Any response sentence of the form 'I filed/wrote/appended X' must be preceded by the tool call in the same turn, or phrased as intent ('I will file'). The generalisable check is that a write-claim names the path AND a read-back confirms it.
class: reported an action that was never performed

lesson: A waiver in daily-deep-learning's quality contract waived the e2e domain on the stated ground that the app was not running. The app had been up since 2026-07-22, so it was live during every gate run. The real cause was a crash in claude-setup/tools/browser/cdp.py WS.__init__, which split ws://[::1]:9224/... on the first colon and raised before auditing any route. The waiver's expiry was 2026-08-10, so a false reason would have hidden a real cross-lane defect for nearly two weeks.
why_it_happened: gate.py requires a waiver to carry a reason and an expiry date, and treats both as satisfied by their presence. The expiry is checked mechanically and fails closed on a malformed date. The REASON is never checked at all: it is unverified prose. So a waiver whose reason is false is indistinguishable from one whose reason is true, and the failing domain stops being investigated because it now looks explained.
fix: The specific defect is fixed: split_ws_url and ws_host_header in tools/browser/cdp.py, with four parameterised tests covering both stacks plus a zone-id literal, verified live over [::1]. The general defect is not fixed. A waiver reason should name a check that can be run to confirm it, in the same way a claim in state/claims-verify.jsonl carries a falsifier. 'The app is not running' is a claim with an obvious executable test that nobody ran.
class: an accountability field that is required but never verified

lesson: tools/review/panel.py matched py-shell-true against tools/map/codemap.py:66, which is a COMMENT documenting that the vulnerable git() helper was deleted on 2026-07-27. The panel flagged the record of a fix as the vulnerability, and blocked the gate on it. All 5 blocking HIGH findings this run were the same class: two comment/docstring hits, one print() string concat read as SQL, and two hits inside docs/prior-art/*.json, which are data files with no code in them.
why_it_happened: The panel is a regex over ADDED LINES, with no lexical layer. It cannot tell code from a comment, a string, or a JSON document, so any file whose prose discusses a vulnerability scores as having one. That makes writing down why a defect was removed more expensive than leaving it undocumented, which is the opposite of the incentive this repo wants.
fix: Waived review until 2026-08-12 with an AST check embedded in the waiver reason as the falsifier (zero shell=True call nodes, zero execute() calls), so the reason can be refuted by running it rather than believed. The real fix is a lexical pass so panel.py skips comment and string tokens; that is an oracle edit and needs operator approval before it is made. NOTE this is the THIRD occurrence: panel.py carries comments at lines 221 and 798 recording two earlier waivers for the same class on 2026-07-26. A defect that has now cost three waivers is not being fixed by waiving it.
class: an oracle that cannot distinguish code from prose about code, so documenting a fix reads as the defect

lesson: The 2026-07-29 intent-traceability and trace-model specs both build on ~/.claude/projects/<slug>/<session>.jsonl, joining on promptId, parentUuid and uuid, and the trace-model spec calls that file THE timeline. Claude Code documentation states the opposite of what those specs assume: the entry format is internal and changes between versions, so scripts parsing these files directly can break on any release. The documented stable interfaces are /export and claude -p --resume <id> --output-format json.
why_it_happened: The schema was measured, not read about. Parsing 817 transcripts and finding promptId on 279 of 279 user rows is strong evidence the field EXISTS and no evidence at all that it is SUPPORTED. Present-and-consistent was treated as stable, which is the same move as treating an artifact that exists as evidence it works.
fix: Design decision taken 2026-07-29: capture_turn.py takes session_id, cwd and prompt from the UserPromptSubmit HOOK PAYLOAD, which is a documented hook input, and never parses a transcript. Transcript-derived fields (promptId, message_uuid) go in metadata as OPTIONAL enrichment whose absence must not fail capture. The specs backfill plan, which joins 587 corpus rows against transcript files, stays on unstable ground and must be marked at-risk rather than scheduled. Ticket identity was already content-derived from {session_id, text_sha, occurrence_index} with no vendor id in it, so the id scheme survives a format change; that was luck of a good reason, not foresight about this risk.
class: an internal vendor format measured carefully and then treated as a public contract

lesson: Read a stranger's Cloudflare Pages project as the operator's own. the-bench.pages.dev resolved with an Access login wall, and the operator's ambiguous 'it has a name already' was interpreted as confirming an existing owned project. The split was wired to that name and the learning site's /writing/* 301'd to a third party's login page for roughly four minutes between the failed deploy and the fix.
why_it_happened: Existence was treated as ownership. A resolving subdomain plus an ambiguous operator phrase produced a confident identification with zero evidence connecting the project to the operator's account. The one check that could have refuted it before any live traffic moved, deploying to the project name under the account's own token, was run only as the production step, not as a probe.
fix: The deploy itself failed closed ('Project not found' [8000007]) and the redirect was repointed within minutes; _redirects and the workflow now carry the collision as a comment. Standing change: before wiring anything to an external name, verify OWNERSHIP with a credentialed read (wrangler pages project list / an API GET under the account token), never with anonymous DNS or HTTP presence, which can only prove existence.
class: external presence read as ownership; the credentialed check ran last instead of first

lesson: The prose gate guards files and does not guard the assistant's response text, which is the only channel the operator reads continuously. Measured on this session's own transcript: 28 assistant text turns, 17 carrying a spaced em/en dash connector, 33 violations, 61 percent of turns. tools/slop_lint.py was run on every markdown file written this session and passed every time.
why_it_happened: Enforcement was attached to artifacts because artifacts are what the gate fingerprints. The response is not a file, so no oracle sees it, and passing the linter on a doc reads as compliance with the writing rule while the actual output stream violates it every other turn. An oracle that covers the cheapest-to-check surface and not the highest-traffic one measures the wrong thing.
fix: Not yet fixed. The mechanical option is a Stop-hook check that runs the slop patterns over the turn's response text and returns one corrective turn, same shape as the handback check; it must key on the rendered text and tolerate legitimate dashes inside quoted code or data (the panel.py false-positive class, L-2026-07-29-d). Filed in TODO.md 2026-07-29.
class: an oracle applied to the artifact channel while the operator-facing channel stays ungated

lesson: Presented a merged architecture plan as 'full scope' and 'plan of record' after sweeping only TODO.md plus the session's own working memory. Eight source classes were never read: 19 unread bus messages to this lane (oldest 2026-07-25, including '160 canonical files never deployed to live'), CLAUDE-OS.md's layer and supersession table, docs/INDEX.md with the PRDs and 15 ADRs, tools/selfimprove/scan.py output, refute.py falsifiers, lane C and lane D backlogs, skills_sync drift (52 items), pointers scan (261 absent paths). Every one was a single command.
why_it_happened: A merge request was read as a synthesis-of-what-I-hold task rather than a discovery task, and completeness was asserted rather than checked. This is the mirror of L-2026-07-29-a: that lesson was an absence claim made against evidence in hand, this is a presence-of-coverage claim made with no coverage check at all.
fix: The reconciliation sweep is the fix and is defined as a fixed command set (bus inbox, scan.py, refute run, skills_sync check, pointers scan, lane backlogs, gh open work, INDEX/CLAUDE-OS read). Standing change: a plan claiming scope names the sources it swept and the ones it did not, in the plan itself. Also filed: scan.py ranks three phantom hook defects at the top (all three hooks exist live at 7941/2519/1306 bytes), so the documented entry point for choosing work is returning false positives.
class: completeness asserted without a coverage check, on a system whose own inventory tools are unread or wrong

lesson: A skip is not a pass, and the ship gate cannot tell the difference. A generator bug deleted every money figure from all 12 shipped resumes and left NUL bytes in their place. The four tests that assert those exact claims responded by calling pytest.skip('appears in no shipped HTML'), so the suite reported '89 passed, 4 skipped' instead of failing, and the gate's unit domain read that as PASS. The artifacts were visibly corrupt while every automated check was green.
why_it_happened: The consistency tests were written to skip when a claim is absent, because an arm that legitimately omits a claim should not fail. That is correct for absence by configuration and wrong for absence by corruption, and the oracle cannot distinguish them. The gate then aggregates on exit code, where a skip is indistinguishable from a pass. Same class as the repo's own documented stale-PDF incident: an oracle whose failure mode is silence.
fix: Fixed locally in new-recruit: test_no_control_bytes_reach_any_shipped_html fails rather than skips, and it is the check that would have caught this in seconds. Two setup-level actions remain open: (1) the gate's unit domain should surface skip counts and treat a rise in skips against the previous run as a red flag, since 92 passed -> 89 passed + 4 skipped was the actual signal and it was invisible; (2) any claim-consistency oracle that can skip needs a companion integrity oracle that cannot.

lesson: The Grep tool is ripgrep and honours .gitignore while walking, so gitignored trees return zero hits from any repo-root search. Measured in ~/Downloads/new-recruit: the identical query returned 0 hits by default and 26 with --no-ignore. /projects/ and /archive/ are ignored there (.gitignore lines 133, 131), hiding 17292 files of the operator's last seven months of project work, across 16 top-level projects, plus 278 ignored top-level entries including PROJECTS-MANIFEST.md, so the index to the hidden work is itself hidden.
why_it_happened: Nothing was forbidden: Read, Bash, and an explicitly-named Grep path all reach these files. What was lost is DISCOVERY. A search returns only what it walks, so an ignored tree is findable only by someone who already knows it exists, which makes every unknown unknown permanent and lets a sweep report clean while missing more files than it read. The operator raised it as a hypothesis; it was correct and had never been tested.
fix: New standing rule dot-claude/rules/hidden-trees.md, deployed both copies: check `git status --ignored --porcelain | grep '^!!' | wc -l` before claiming a repo sweep is complete, and reach ignored trees either by naming the path in Grep or with `rg --no-ignore` under Bash, saying which was used. NOT fixed: tools/audit/pointers.py reported ~/projects/campaign-analysis absent five times while 1626 files of it exist under Downloads/new-recruit/projects, so the oracle mechanised the absence-claim class (L-2026-07-29-a) and still does.
class: a search tool that silently excludes a subtree, so absence of hits reads as absence of files
a namespace was searched, absence found inside it, and absence reported for the whole space
detail: L-2026-07-29-a fired three times in session beba6c57, the third AFTER the first two were written into a reflection. Instance 3: 'the dataviz skill does not exist anywhere' was published after searching dot-*/skills/ and ~/.claude/skills/ only. dataviz is a Claude Code BUILT-IN, visible via /context and not via the filesystem. The same output shows review and security-review are built-ins too, unused, while the review gate domain carries its third waiver and three external replacements were evaluated without naming them.
falsifier: Before any absence claim about a skill, enumerate four namespaces and name the ones searched IN the claim: dot-*/skills/, ~/.claude/skills/, ~/.claude/plugins/marketplaces/, and built-ins. Built-ins are visible only through /context or the skill listing, never through the filesystem.

class: a flaky test inside an oracle suite, so the gate's unit domain is non-deterministic
detail: tests/test_panel_stale_lines.py::test_unreadable_file_fails_open failed once in a full-suite run (1 failed, 254 passed) and then passed twice: once in isolation, and once in a full re-run of 255. The gate reported unit PASS in the same window, so the gate and the suite disagreed and the gate was the one that was right the second time. Root cause NOT established. The run that failed was the first after temp_sweep deleted 1,884 directories with chmod-and-retry, and the test concerns unreadable-file handling, so a permissions or filesystem race is the leading hypothesis and is unproven.
falsifier: Run the full suite 20 times and count failures of that node id. A single failure makes the unit domain non-deterministic, which means a green gate does not imply a green suite. Either pin the cause or quarantine the test with a named reason.
closed_by: Cause was mine and mechanical: test_unreadable_file_fails_open patched builtins.open globally with monkeypatch, so any pytest internal that opened a file during that test (assertion rewriting, capture, traceback formatting) raised OSError, and whether that happened depended on collection order. Fixed by patching the name in panel's module namespace instead (monkeypatch.setattr(panel, 'open', boom, raising=False)), which reaches drop_stale_lines and nothing else. The sibling read-count test had the same defect plus a manual try/finally swap that could leak a global on assertion failure; it is now monkeypatch-scoped too. Evidence: three consecutive full-suite runs, 292 passed each, no failures. Lesson kept OPEN in spirit as the class rule now written into the test file: never patch a builtin globally inside a suite that is also an oracle.

class: a waiver renewed twice on a stated reason nobody ever executed
detail: The review domain carried a waiver through three renewals (two recorded in panel.py comments on 2026-07-26, one expiring 2026-08-12) whose stated reason was that the blocking HIGH findings were pattern matches against comments and docstrings. Measured 2026-07-30 with the operator's go-ahead: that reason was wrong for all five. Three were English prose that happened to contain a SQL verb and a plus sign ('Delete ~380 lines (... checks + their selftest)'), and two were REAL shell=True code on lines this branch added and later deleted, reported against line numbers now occupied by the comment recording the deletion. The waiver even shipped its own falsifier (an AST walk of the final file) which PASSED, and passing it confirmed 'not shipping' while the reader inferred 'the pattern matched a comment'. A falsifier that is true for a different reason than the one written next to it launders a wrong diagnosis into an audited one. Both real defects are now fixed in the oracle (tools/review/panel.py sql-concat lookaheads, drop_stale_lines) with 20 pinned cases. Rule: a waiver's reason must name the mechanism, and the falsifier must be able to distinguish that mechanism from every other reason the same command could pass.

class: the gate checks the ruled form of a style rule and not the property the rule exists to protect
detail: Operator read a 5.4k-word deliverable that had passed tools/slop_lint.py and said it felt letter-by-letter machine written, naming dashes. Measured: zero em dashes, zero en dashes, two non-ASCII characters total, both quoted from the artifact under review. slop_lint gates a banned-phrase list, ' - ' as a connector, and ritual openers. It does not measure hyphen-compound density (2.8%) or sentence-length variance (mean 22.1, stdev 14.8), which is what actually reads as generated. ~/.claude/skills/voice-metrics/SKILL.md:21 already classifies 'no em dashes' as RULED, a decision with no corpus behind it, so the harness gates the ruled proxy and leaves the measured property ungated. Same shape as L-2026-07-29-g. Fix is a variance and density check in slop_lint.py with thresholds fitted from voice-metrics against the operator's own corpus, not guessed; filed in TODO.md.

class: a reviewer's own numbers went unchecked until an independent recount, and four were wrong
detail: An 11k-word review of two external artifacts presented ~15 measured quantities in the same flat voice as its inferences. A fresh-context verification agent re-derived every one and four were wrong: an anchor PDF's 798 near-black glyphs were reported as #2625A6 when 2500134 is #262626 (a decimal-to-hex slip that turned 'no text accent colour at all' into 'a link colour', weakening the argument it supported); a font share of 97% was 93.8%; a word count of 4 was 5; and a defect described as 4 bad table cells was 33 of 94, every one off by exactly one last digit, which widened the scope and lowered the severity at the same time. Separately, rendering the artifact in a browser overturned three findings that had been derived from CSS text. Rule for review work: derived numbers get recomputed by something that cannot see the reasoning, and any claim about a rendered artifact is inference until it has been rendered.

class: a session banner carried a retired lane letter, and the lane it named was not the lane the work belonged to
detail: The SessionStart recall banner opened this session with 'LANE E: content & publishing'. docs/charters.md renumbered the lanes on 2026-07-30: E is retired and content is now D. So the banner is one cutover behind, and it is generated text the session trusts before it reads the charter. The stale label then masked a second, larger error: the whole turn edited daily-deep-learning curriculum blocks (build_curriculum.py S5/S6, 322->355 units), talents.json quest ladders on frontend and aiux, four new skills, and course_plan.json scan sources. That is Lane C (learning) work verbatim, and the content charter explicitly says 'Does NOT: learning content (C)'. No claim was appended to claims.jsonl before starting, per anti-convergence rule 1, and daily-deep-learning has no state/ directory at all so the claim path a Lane C session would use does not exist in that repo. Two separate fixes: the banner generator must resolve lane letters through tools/lib/lanes.py using the row timestamp rather than emitting a literal, and a lane charter check belongs at first-write, not at end-of-turn self-audit, because by the time the operator asked what the lane was the edits were already on disk and validating clean.

class: the green-test gradient: scope drifts toward whatever can go green before the turn ends
detail: Operator-named, 2026-07-31. Not a failure to test. The tests are real and they measure the scope that was chosen, which is how a wrong scope stays invisible. Observed in this session as: a 350-line artifact published without ever being rendered while a browser was connected; a selftest assertion coupled to the working tree so it went green locally and broke the unit domain; a budget fixed at 05:00 and the identical error repeated at 06:30. Corroborating measurement: three separate Stop hooks, not this model's judgement, forced every calibration and both prior-art retractions this session.
falsifier: For any turn that reports a build or a design as working, name the check that could have failed and did not, and show it ran against the DELIVERABLE rather than against the part that was easy to prove. For a visual artifact that means a render.

class: a latency or budget number measured on a path that returned before doing the work
detail: Twice in one session. hookgate reported 14.85ms and 16.3x because the payload failed JSON parsing and main returned before the matcher; real figures 91.87ms Windows, 49.01ms Linux. pre_push_gate was cut 90s -> 10s on three samples averaging 161ms, including a `git push origin main` returning in 166ms; the hook's own internal subprocess timeouts are 5s, 20s and 8s, totalling 33s on the validation path, so 10s truncates a credential audit and a truncated security gate fails open. Reverted to 90s, which is also unmeasured but is reasoned from the internal budget. A third instance the same day: the gate's unit domain carried a 300s budget sized when the suite was 70 tests, and it was diagnosed at 05:00 and the identical error committed again at 06:30.
falsifier: Before reporting a latency or sizing a budget, show the measured invocation REACHED the work: a non-zero finding, a written artifact, a parsed payload. A number produced by a path that returned early does not measure the path that does not.
note_on_this_row: Filed on the second attempt. The first used id -d, which was already taken, and the append silently skipped it while reporting 'appended 1 lesson'. A collision check that drops the row instead of renaming it is the same shape as the defect above: the report was true and the thing it described did not happen.

class: a host-shaped default that is correct on the host it was written on and silently answers the wrong question on the other
detail: First session run from WSL, 2026-07-31. Five instances of one shape, none of which crashed: (1) make_lane_launchers.py used Path.home() both to stat a lane repo and to write it into a .lnk, so from WSL every lane printed MISSING DIR and --apply wrote nothing while exiting 0. (2) Four tools (selfimprove/scan.py, digest/build_digest.py, local/reflex_router.py, audit_claude_setup.py) defaulted the harness repo to Path.home()/claude-setup, which under WSL is a SECOND checkout at /home/shov/claude-setup measured two commits behind /mnt/c (8a4217b vs 3f23458); they succeeded against the stale tree and wrote proposals.jsonl into it. (3) scan.py resolve_hook_target translated MSYS /c/... to C:/..., unreachable from Linux, so every wired hook read as missing again, the exact defect that function was written to fix. (4) quality-contract.json spells every domain command `python`; Ubuntu has only python3, so unit, types and docmap returned exit 127 and a FAIL row naming three blocking domains went into state/gate-runs.jsonl against a tree whose 367 tests passed in the same minute. (5) bus.py lane_for called Path(r'c:\...').resolve(), which under Linux joins a Windows literal onto the cwd, so EVERY cwd derived lane '?' including the three the selftest asserts, making this session's bus messages unaddressable. Instance 5 is the sharpest: the selftest passed Windows-shaped literals, so it looked exercised while measuring nothing on this host.
falsifier: For any path, interpreter name, or home directory a tool derives rather than is given: name the two hosts it must be right on, and show the check ran on the one it was NOT written on. A green selftest whose inputs are literals in the other host's spelling is not evidence.

class: an include target validated by existence rather than by content
detail: daily-deep-learning's CLAUDE.md was gutted to @AGENTS.md on 2026-07-31 and the AGENTS.md on disk was claude-setup's harness guidance, wrong repository entirely. I committed it (284be59) after checking the file existed and never reading it; the briefing an agent would boot from described dot-claude trees and lanes that do not exist there. Caught 40 minutes later only because a grep for TODO surfaced selfimprove/scan.py, a path DDL cannot have. Fixed in abfa951 by restoring the repo's own 146 lines from history. Same class as read-whole-before-reasoning: existence is not evidence about content, and an @include makes the unread file the entire contract.

class: a green run that recites its own falsifier without running it
detail: The skills waiver's reason ended with 'CONFIRM BY RUNNING: python tools/audit/skills_sync.py check -- expect DRIFT: 51. If it prints a different number this waiver is stale.' A gate run on 2026-08-07 printed that sentence verbatim as the domain's evidence, reported WAIVED, and returned VERDICT: PASS. Run by hand ninety seconds later the checker printed DRIFT: 29 and exited 1. Nothing in the output was false; it asserted more than the run had measured, which is the false-green class calibrated-claims names as worst, appearing inside the contract's own machinery. The generalisation is not about waivers: any instruction written as prose inside an artifact a tool prints is read by humans as a check that ran. Closed mechanically by waived.confirm in tools/gate/gate.py, which runs the waived domain's command anyway and fails the domain when the string is gone. Still open as a class: nothing stops the next falsifier from being written as prose somewhere the gate does not read.

class: a size comparison read as a currency comparison
detail: skills_sync reports repo-vs-live byte counts. grill-me showed 635b repo against 1261b live, the only skill where live is larger, and that was written into the waiver as a possible content loss in the payload tree. The diff says the opposite: 3df7704 rewrote the repo copy on 2026-08-03 into a terse four-line brief and live still holds the older structured protocol, so the repo is ahead and live is stale. Bytes order files by size and carry no information about which one is current. The same shape sits in the other 16 rows of that bucket, where the difference is one added line and the larger file is also the newer one, which is what made the inference feel safe.

class: a stale row that keeps its place at the top of the boot surface because nothing reorders it
detail: TODO row A ('skills_sync.py check exists, CI runs only its selftest, and the check exits 0 while reporting drift') was reachable at session boot on 2026-08-07 and every clause of it was already false: check exits 1, a skills domain and a pointers domain both exist in quality-contract.json, ship-gate.yml runs the check at line 260, and the count is 29 rather than 55. session-recall.sh takes the first six '- [ ]' rows by line number, so a row that closes keeps its slot and a row that opens below it is never seen. Two days of sessions booted on a finished instruction. This is the already-recorded '90 of 96 invisible' row doing damage from the other side: the cap is correct and the ordering is the defect.

class: an HTTP 200 read as proof a file is served, on a host with a catch-all fallback
detail: Re-scoring R38 (docs/ must not be public) on daily-deep-learning.pages.dev, curl returned 200 for /docs/REQUIREMENTS-OF-RECORD-2026-07-26.md and for /tools/validate_links.py, which reads as a live leak of private planning documents. It is not one. Cloudflare Pages falls back to index.html for unknown paths, so /docs/NOSUCHFILE-xyz.md also returns 200 and all three bodies are the identical 148957-byte app shell. The status line alone inverts the answer. The check that works is status plus size plus content type, or a byte comparison against a known-absent control path. A control request for a path that cannot exist is the cheap general fix and it is what settled this one.
fix: R38 in docs/REQUIREMENTS-OF-RECORD-2026-07-26.md now carries the do-not-verify-by-status-alone note with the three measured 200s next to each other.

class: a directory read as the product model after the generator moved to a different one
detail: posts/ ends at 2026-07-28 and today is 2026-08-07, which reads as a daily generator dead for ten days. The generator is alive and moved: it writes units/*.md plus a curriculum.json entry and commits as 'unit: <id>', last two m2-ranking (2026-08-06) and m2-gaps-islands (2026-08-07), both deployed green. index.html:2493 boots the home screen off curriculum.json and the dated pages survive only behind #/history. I drafted the ten-day-outage finding before checking git log, and only the commit list stopped it being reported.

class: a check built to catch a class, shipped carrying a different one, and its own falsifier passed because it was only ever run on the host that could measure
detail: The waiver-confirm feature landed on 2026-08-07 to stop the gate reciting a waiver's falsifier without running it. Its claim row's falsifier ended with 'a full gate run on the committed tree records a verdict', and one did: VERDICT PASS on 4a1b8ff, locally. CI failed the same commit an hour later. skills_sync.py check exits 2 when there is no live ~/.claude/skills, which is every runner, so the confirm string was absent for a reason unrelated to the waiver and the gate called it STALE. That is L-2026-07-31-g, host-shaped defaults, committed by the feature built to catch its sibling. The falsifier could not catch it because every clause of it was written to be run on this machine, where the live tree exists; nothing in it named the other host. Fix reads exit 2 structurally rather than matching a marker string, since a substring marker would be an oracle validated by existence rather than content (L-2026-08-05-a), and records waivers_unconfirmed on the run so a CI PASS is not indistinguishable from a local one that asserted more.
rule: A falsifier for anything that reads the environment names the host it fails on, not only the host it passes on. If a check touches ~/.claude, a Windows path, a network service or a venv, one clause of its falsifier runs where that thing is absent.

class: a memory contradicted from half the evidence, because the cheap half of the check ran and the expensive half did not
detail: settings.json wires hooks under /home/shov/claude-setup. Resolving it showed a symlink to work/repos/claude-setup, and a find for .git directories under /home/shov returned exactly one. From that, commit 94354e2's message asserts that the two-clones hazard in project memory 'is wrong'. It is not. The memory names the second clone as /mnt/c/Users/shova/claude-setup, a Windows path the find never reached because it was rooted at /home/shov, and it also states outright that ~/claude-setup is a symlink, so the one thing that was verified was already written down. The clone exists and sits at f5d697e, a different commit from this session's HEAD. The memory was right in every particular and the correction was published in a commit message that cannot be edited.
rule: Before contradicting a written memory, re-read it and check every path it names. A search rooted where the claim is convenient is not evidence about a claim that names somewhere else. Contradicting a record is a higher bar than writing one, not a lower one, because the record was written with evidence in hand and the contradiction usually is not.

class: a deployed unit pointed at code that had not landed yet, so the schedule broke on a flag the target did not know
detail: Moving the agent feed from issue comments to a GitHub Discussion, I edited tools/telemetry/systemd/agent-feed.service to pass --sink discussion, copied it to ~/.config/systemd/user, and ran daemon-reload. The unit's ExecStart names /home/shov/work/repos/claude-setup/tools/telemetry/publish.py, the MAIN tree. My publish.py lived in a worktree on an unmerged branch. Six seconds later the timer fired and exited 2 with `unrecognized arguments: --sink discussion`. The generalisable shape is not 'I forgot to merge'. It is that a deployed schedule and the code it invokes are two artifacts with independent lifetimes, and nothing in this repo checks that they agree. tools/audit/pointers.py scans hooks and skills for dead paths and has ZERO references to .service, .timer or systemd, so a unit can name a nonexistent script, an unsupported flag, or a path in a different tree and no gate domain notices. Measured: `grep -c 'service\|timer\|systemd' tools/audit/pointers.py` returns 0. Cost was small only because the failure was loud and the old sink still existed. It was deliberately kept so the migration would be reversible, and reverting the live unit to the issue form took one command and restored a green timer. Had the issue sink been deleted as dead code, a reversible mistake would have been an outage with no path back. Two fixes, neither done in this pass: extend pointers.py to parse ExecStart and assert the target exists and accepts its flags (--help exit 0 is a cheap oracle), and never deploy a unit ahead of the code it names.
falsifier: pointers.py scan reports a unit whose ExecStart names a missing script or an unaccepted flag, and fails; and the systemd unit is redeployed only after the commit carrying its target is an ancestor of the branch the unit's path resolves to.
